questions.q: The Hampi Bazaar of the Vijayanagara Empire was located opposite which temple?
questions.a: The Virupaksha temple: the chapter says the Hampi Bazaar was located opposite it.

questions.q: Which Portuguese traveller called Hampi 'the best-provided city in the world'?
questions.a: Domingos Paes, who praised the wide variety of products traded in its market. Fernao Nuniz was another Portuguese traveller who wrote about the bazaar, but the phrase is Paes's.

questions.q: Look at three events. (i) A carpet maker in Bhadohi sells a carpet to a buyer in Germany and is paid for it. (ii) Two farmers in a village exchange a sack of wheat for a sack of potatoes. (iii) A family cooks rice from its own field for its own dinner. Going by the chapter's meaning of trade, which of these are trade?
o: (i) only, because trade must involve payment in money
(ii) only, because trade takes place only between people of the same country
(i), (ii) and (iii), because goods are used in all three
questions.a: (i) and (ii) only. The chapter defines trade as buying and selling or exchange of goods and services between people or countries: (i) is buying and selling between people of two countries, and (ii) is an exchange of goods between people. In (iii) nothing is bought, sold or exchanged with anyone.

questions.q: True or False? 'Markets do more than make goods and services available; they also connect people, traditions and ideas.' Give the verdict and one example of a market from the chapter that does this.
questions.a: True. Besides making goods and services available, markets connect people, traditions and ideas. Example: at Ima Keithal in Imphal, people from different communities come together to exchange ideas and enjoy shared traditions.
s: States the verdict: True
Gives an example such as Ima Keithal, where people from different communities exchange ideas and share traditions

questions.q: In economics, what is the difference between a need and a want? Give one example of each.
questions.a: A need is something a person requires to survive, such as food, water, clothing or shelter. A want is something a person desires but is not essential for survival, such as a toy car or a fancy watch.
s: Need: something required to survive, with an example such as food, water, clothing or shelter
Want: something desired but not essential for survival, with a suitable example

questions.q: Answer briefly from the chapter: (a) Give two other names by which a market is known. (b) Hampi Bazaar was one of the prosperous markets of which empire? (c) Name any two goods that Domingos Paes saw traded in Hampi.
questions.a: (a) Any two of: bazaar, haat (Hindi), marukatte (Kannada). (b) The Vijayanagara Empire. (c) Any two of: grains, seeds, milk, oil, silk, animals such as cows, rabbits and horses, birds such as quails and partridges.
s: Gives two names for a market, such as bazaar and haat or marukatte
Names the Vijayanagara Empire
Names two goods from Paes's list, such as grains and silk

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Fernao Nuniz found the abundance of goods in the Hampi Bazaar a mystery.
Reason (R): Nuniz described the country around Hampi as barren.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: Nuniz wrote that it was so barren a country that it was a mystery how there should be an abundance of everything in the bazaar.

questions.q: Look at three events. (i) Rohit gives his old cricket bat to his cousin as a birthday gift. (ii) At a Sunday haat, Meena buys 2 kg of onions from a vendor at Rs 30 per kg, the price they both agreed on. (iii) Ravi reaches the haat late to buy a clay lamp, but the only potter has already packed up and gone home, so Ravi leaves with nothing. Which of these is a completed market transaction? Explain each case using the features of a market.
questions.a: Only (ii) is a completed market transaction: there is a buyer, a seller and a price both agreed on. (i) is not: it is a gift, with no buyer, no seller and no price. (iii) is not: Ravi was a buyer, but no seller was present, so no price could be agreed and no transaction took place.
s: Identifies (ii) as the completed transaction because buyer and seller agreed on a price
Explains that (i) is a gift with no buying, selling or price
Explains that in (iii) there was no seller, so no price was agreed and no transaction took place

questions.q:
Every Thursday a weekly market is held in a village near Mysuru, Karnataka. It has 12 vegetable sellers, 6 grain sellers, 4 sellers of perfume, 2 bangle sellers and 1 potter. One Thursday, Lakshmi buys 3 kg of rice at Rs 50 per kg from a grain seller. The potter sits at his stall all day but sells nothing.
(a) The chapter gives the Kannada name for a market. What is it?
(b) From the stalls, name one good that meets a need and one that meets a want.
(c) Food is a need. How many of all the stalls sell food, and what percentage of all the stalls is this?
(d) A visitor says, 'The potter was not part of the market that day, because he sold nothing.' Do you agree? Give a reason.
questions.a: (a) Marukatte. (b) Need: rice, grain or vegetables (food is needed to survive); want: perfume or bangles (desired but not essential for survival). (c) 12 + 6 = 18 of the 25 stalls (12 + 6 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 25) sell food, which is 18/25 = 72%. (d) No. A market is a place where people buy and sell; the potter was a seller offering goods there. Making no sale only means no buyer agreed on a price with him that day; he was still part of the market.
s: (a) Marukatte
(b) Names a need such as rice or vegetables and a want such as perfume or bangles
(c) 18 food stalls out of 25, that is 72%
(d) Disagrees: the potter was a seller offering goods in the market; no sale only means no agreed price that day

questions.q: In the chapter's guava example, at what price per kg does the price of guavas finally settle as 'just right' for both buyer and seller?
questions.a: Rs 40 per kg: not very high for the buyer and not too low for the seller. Rs 80 was too high and Rs 20 too low.

questions.q: A guava seller fixes a very high price for his guavas. According to the chapter, what is most likely to happen?
o: Buyers may not be willing to buy at that price, so many guavas stay unsold
Every buyer pays the price at once, because guavas are needed
The government fixes a lower price for him the same day
Buyers pay more to show they value his guavas
questions.a: Buyers may not be willing to buy at that price: a buyer who finds the price very high asks for a lower one, and if no agreeable price is reached the sale does not take place.

questions.q:
Match each term in Column I with its meaning in Column II.
Column I: 1. Price  2. Supply  3. Demand  4. Trade
Column II: P. Quantity of a product that consumers are willing and able to purchase at a particular price at a given time  Q. The amount at which a buyer is willing to buy and a seller is willing to sell particular goods or services  R. Quantity of a product that sellers are willing and able to sell at a particular price at a given time  S. Buying and selling or exchange of goods and services between people or countries
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: Price = the amount at which buyer and seller are both willing to deal; supply = what sellers are willing and able to sell at a price; demand = what consumers are willing and able to buy at a price; trade = buying, selling or exchange between people or countries.

questions.q:
Lata sells bananas at a weekly market. Use the chapter's guava example to answer.
(a) She asks a very high price. What are most buyers likely to do?
(b) She asks a very low price. Why may she not want to do this?
(c) What do Lata and a buyer usually do when they do not agree on her first price?
(d) Over some weeks she finds a price at which most of her bananas sell and she still gains. How does the chapter describe such a price?
(e) What can Lata learn from these weeks for her next visit to the market?
questions.a: (a) Many buyers will not buy at that price and will ask for a lower one. (b) At a very low price she would lose; it would not be profitable for her. (c) They negotiate or bargain until a mutually agreeable price is reached. (d) A price that is just right: high enough for the seller and low enough for the buyer. (e) She can judge roughly what quantity of bananas buyers need and bring about that quantity next time.
s: (a) Buyers will not buy at a very high price and ask for less
(b) A very low price means a loss, not profitable for the seller
(c) They negotiate or bargain to reach a mutually agreeable price
(d) The just-right price: high enough for the seller, low enough for the buyer
(e) She learns roughly what quantity buyers need and offers that quantity in future

questions.q: At a school book fair, an atlas is priced at Rs 250. Of the 60 students who look at it, 45 would like to buy it, but only 30 of these 45 have Rs 250 with them. Another 5 students have the money but do not want the atlas. Going by the chapter's meaning of demand, what is the demand for the atlas at Rs 250 at the fair that day?
questions.a: 30 copies. Demand is the quantity that consumers are willing and able to purchase at a particular price at a given time. Only the 30 students who both want the atlas and can pay Rs 250 count; the other 15 who want it cannot pay, and the 5 who can pay do not want it.

questions.q:
Consider these statements about prices in a market.
I. A seller who fixes a very low price may make no profit.
II. Once a seller has fixed a price, buyers can never change it by bargaining.
III. Over time, the quantity offered by sellers and the quantity needed by buyers help determine the price.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. A very low price is not profitable for the seller, and over time the amounts offered and needed help fix a just-right price. II is wrong: buyers and sellers often negotiate and bargain to reach an acceptable price.

questions.q: In Ahmedabad, Imran brought 300 kites to sell on the day before Makar Sankranti. At Rs 20 each, all 300 were sold by noon, and about 100 more buyers, each wanting one kite, went home without one. He kept 60 more kites for the day after the festival: at Rs 20 only 5 sold, and at Rs 8 he sold 25 more. (a) Using the idea of demand, explain why buyers accepted Rs 20 before the festival. (b) How many kites were left unsold after the festival, and what does this show about demand then? (c) How many kites should he bring for the day before the festival next year, and about how many for the day after? Show your working.
questions.a: (a) Before the festival many buyers were willing and able to buy kites at Rs 20; more buyers wanted kites than he had, so they accepted his price. (b) 60 - 5 - 25 = 30 kites were left unsold: after the festival few buyers wanted kites, so demand fell and even Rs 8 could not sell them all. (c) Before the festival: 300 + 100 = about 400 kites, since about 100 buyers went without one. After the festival: only about 5 + 25 = 30 kites, the number that actually sold. The chapter says a seller learns approximately what quantity buyers need and offers that quantity in future.
s: (a) Explains high demand before the festival, with more buyers than kites
(b) 30 unsold kites, showing that demand fell after the festival
(c) About 400 before (300 + 100) and about 30 after (5 + 25), using the seller learning the quantity buyers need

questions.q: Gopal buys 40 kg of fresh spinach at Rs 15 per kg for the weekly market. By 7 pm he has sold 28 kg at Rs 30 per kg. Spinach left over will wilt and be thrown away. For the last 12 kg he has two plans. Plan A: cut the price to Rs 12 per kg, and late-night buyers will take all 12 kg. Plan B: keep Rs 30 per kg; he will sell only 2 kg more. (a) Find his total profit or loss on the 40 kg under each plan. (b) Rs 12 is below the Rs 15 he paid. Why may he still accept it? (c) Why do many buyers wait until late at night to buy vegetables? (d) Which plan should Gopal choose? Justify, using the data and the chapter's idea of a price acceptable to both buyer and seller.
questions.a: (a) Cost: 40 x 15 = Rs 600; sales till 7 pm: 28 x 30 = Rs 840. Plan A: 840 + 12 x 12 = Rs 984, profit Rs 384. Plan B: 840 + 2 x 30 = Rs 900, profit Rs 300. (b) The money for the spinach is already spent; unsold spinach wilts and earns nothing, so Rs 12 a kg is better than Rs 0 for the last 12 kg. (c) Late at night the price is lower, and buyers ask for a price they are willing to pay; they know sellers want to clear perishable stock. (d) Plan A: it earns Rs 84 more (Rs 384 against Rs 300). A price is reached when buyer and seller both accept it: at night Rs 12 suits buyers, and it suits Gopal better than letting the spinach wilt.
s: (a) Plan A profit Rs 384 and Plan B profit Rs 300 (cost Rs 600, day sales Rs 840)
(b) Unsold spinach earns nothing, so a low price still brings in more than wasting it
(c) Buyers get a lower price late at night, a price they are willing to pay
(d) Chooses Plan A (Rs 84 more), a price both buyers and the seller accept at that hour

questions.q: India was the world's largest importer of vegetable oils in 2024. From which countries is most of India's palm oil imported?
questions.a: Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand, according to the chapter.

questions.q: Which of these purchases takes place in a physical market?
o: Sana buys a mobile phone at a store in a mall and pays for it with a phone app
Raju orders groceries on an app and they are delivered to his door
Priya pays for and joins an online drawing class from home
Vikram buys a book on a website and it reaches him the next day
questions.a: Sana's purchase: she meets the seller in person at a mall store, so it is a physical market even though she pays through an app. The others are online transactions in which buyer and seller never meet.

questions.q:
Match each example in Column I with the type of market in Column II.
Column I: 1. Families shopping at stores inside a multi-storey mall  2. Buying a laptop through a shopping app  3. Paper for this textbook bought from paper mills in India  4. India buying palm oil from Malaysia
Column II: P. Domestic market  Q. Online market  R. Physical market  S. International market
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: A mall is a physical market; a shopping app is an online market; paper bought within India is a domestic market; palm oil from Malaysia is an import in an international market.

questions.q: True or False? 'When buyers in one country buy products made in another country and bring them in, they are importing.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter defines import as buying goods or services from other countries and bringing them into one's own country.
s: States the verdict: True
Gives the chapter's meaning of import: buying from other countries and bringing the goods in

questions.q: Name any two kinds of physical market described in the chapter.
questions.a: Any two of: weekly markets or haats where vendors sell vegetables and handicrafts from carts; local markets with shops and street-food vendors; malls, the multi-storey buildings with stores inside.
s: Names one physical market, such as a weekly market or haat
Names a second, such as a local market with shops or a mall

questions.q: (a) What is a domestic market? (b) What is an export? (c) Name one product that India imports, as given in the chapter, and the region it comes from.
questions.a: (a) A market where goods and services are bought and sold within the geographical boundaries of the country. (b) Selling goods or services produced in one country to a buyer in another country. (c) For example, vegetable oils such as palm oil from South East Asia (Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand).
s: (a) Domestic market: buying and selling within the country's boundaries
(b) Export: selling goods or services made in one country to a buyer in another
(c) Names an import with its region, such as palm oil from South East Asia

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Every online market is an international market.
Reason (R): Through apps and websites, buyers and sellers can transact even when they are thousands of kilometres apart.
Choose the correct option.
o: A is false, but R is true
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
questions.a: A is false, but R is true. Online buyers and sellers can be far apart, but if both are within India the sale is in the domestic market; a market is international only when goods cross a country's borders.

questions.q: A student writes, 'India's trade with North America is only in goods that are shipped across the ocean.' Which correction fits Fig. 12.10 of the chapter?
o: India exports outsourced services like software to North America and imports aircraft and components from it
India imports software from North America and exports aircraft to it
India has no trade at all with North America
India only imports vegetable oils from North America
questions.a: Fig. 12.10 shows India exporting outsourced services like software to North America, which is a service, not shipped goods, and importing aircraft and components from it.

questions.q:
A brassware maker in Moradabad, Uttar Pradesh, sold 500 pieces last month. He sold 250 pieces to customers who came to his own shop, 150 pieces through a shopping app to buyers in other Indian states, and 100 pieces to a buyer in Germany who placed the order by e-mail and never visited.
(a) Which of these sales took place in a physical market?
(b) How many pieces did he sell in the domestic market?
(c) What percentage of his pieces were exported?
(d) He plans to close his shop and sell only through the app. Give one reason from the chapter why this may not be wise.
questions.a: (a) The 250 pieces sold to customers at his own shop, where buyer and seller meet in person. (b) 250 + 150 = 400 pieces, since both the shop and app sales are within India. (c) 100 out of 500 = 20%. (d) The physical market is still the most common type of market, and many buyers want to see and handle a product before buying; closing the shop could lose those local customers.
s: (a) The 250 shop sales, where buyer and seller meet in person
(b) 400 pieces in the domestic market (250 + 150)
(c) 20% exported (100 of 500)
(d) A sound reason, such as the physical market being the most common type or buyers wanting to see goods before buying

questions.q: What are the large warehouses called in which wholesalers store grains, vegetables and fruits bought from farms?
questions.a: Godowns: the chapter says the produce is stored in large warehouses called godowns before it is brought to the mandis.

questions.q: Which city has Asia's oldest textile market, according to the chapter?
questions.a: Surat, Gujarat, which is famously known as a textile hub.

questions.q: A wholesaler buys 5 tonnes of wheat and 2 tonnes of fresh green peas from farms. He will send both to the mandi only after three weeks. Going by the chapter, where should he store each?
o: Wheat in an ordinary godown and peas in cold storage, because peas are perishable
Both in cold storage, because all farm produce spoils within three weeks
Both in an ordinary godown, because cold storage is meant only for factory goods
Wheat in cold storage and peas in an ordinary godown, because grain is worth more
questions.a: Wheat in an ordinary godown and peas in cold storage. Grains are stored in large warehouses called godowns; for perishables the warehouses also have cold storage, specialised warehouses kept at low temperatures to preserve perishable goods.

questions.q:
Consider these statements about the supply chain.
I. Wholesalers buy goods in large quantities from producers or manufacturers.
II. Retailers sell in smaller quantities, and their goods are meant for consumption rather than resale.
III. Distributors sell goods directly to final consumers in place of retailers.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and II only. III is wrong: distributors supply goods from manufacturers and wholesalers to retailers, bridging the gap of distance and terrain; they do not replace retailers.

questions.q: Give two differences between a wholesaler and a retailer.
questions.a: (1) A wholesaler buys in large quantities from producers or manufacturers, while a retailer sells in smaller quantities. (2) A wholesaler supplies shops and stores, while a retailer sells to final consumers for consumption rather than resale.
s: Difference in quantity: wholesaler deals in large quantities, retailer in smaller ones
Difference in buyer: wholesaler supplies shops, retailer sells to final consumers for consumption

questions.q: Potatoes grown on a farm near Agra reach a family in Lucknow through a physical market. Using the chapter's chain of supply, answer: (a) Who buys the potatoes from the farm in large quantities? (b) Where are they stored, and what extra facility may be used because they are perishable? (c) To which market are they then brought? (d) Who finally sells them to the family, and in what quantity?
questions.a: (a) A wholesaler buys them in large quantities from the farm. (b) They are stored in large warehouses called godowns, which may have cold storage to keep perishables fresh. (c) They are brought to a mandi, the wholesale market. (d) A retailer, such as a vegetable shop near the family's home, sells them in small quantities for the family to eat.
s: (a) A wholesaler buys in bulk from the farm
(b) Godowns or warehouses, with cold storage for perishables
(c) The mandi or wholesale market
(d) A retailer sells in small quantities to the family as final consumers

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Wholesalers help ensure an uninterrupted supply of products to end consumers.
Reason (R): Wholesalers assess how much product retailers require, which helps maintain the stock of products with the manufacturers.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: by assessing what retailers need, wholesalers help keep stock with manufacturers, and this ensures supply to end consumers does not break.

questions.q: A visitor to Surat says, 'In Surat, raw cotton goes into one big factory and comes out as a saree. No other market is involved.' Use the chapter to give three reasons why this is not correct.
questions.a: (1) Raw cotton reaches Surat through cotton mandis from nearby states like Maharashtra and other parts of Gujarat, so a market is involved before processing. (2) The cotton passes through several stages in different units, such as weaving on power looms and dyeing in processing units. (3) The product moves from stage to stage through markets, for woven fabric, dyed fabric and finished products, and finished goods are then traded in the wholesale market.
s: Raw cotton arrives through cotton mandis from Maharashtra and Gujarat
Processing happens in separate stages and units, such as weaving and dyeing
Goods move between stages through markets and are finally traded in the wholesale market

questions.q:
A wooden-toy maker in Channapatna, Karnataka, makes 5,000 toys a month. He sells 3,000 toys to a wholesaler in Bengaluru, who supplies 60 toy shops across the state. The remaining 2,000 toys go to the warehouse of a company that sells through a shopping app and delivers to buyers' homes.
(a) On average, how many toys does each of the 60 shops get from the wholesaler?
(b) What does the chapter call the app company, and what does it do with his toys?
(c) Some of the 60 shops are in hill towns far from Bengaluru. Who in the chain can help reach them, and why are they needed?
(d) The wholesaler pays him Rs 120 a toy. The app company pays Rs 150 a toy but charges him Rs 40 a toy for packing and delivery. Which channel earns him more per toy? He is thinking of sending all 5,000 toys to the app. Should he? Show your working.
questions.a: (a) 3,000 / 60 = 50 toys per shop. (b) An aggregator: it holds his toys in its warehouse, combines them with offers from other sellers, and packs and delivers each order to the online buyer. (c) Distributors: distances and difficult terrain make it hard for a wholesaler to reach many retailers, and distributors bridge this gap. (d) Wholesaler: Rs 120 a toy; app: 150 - 40 = Rs 110 a toy, so the wholesaler channel earns more per toy. Now he earns 3,000 x 120 + 2,000 x 110 = Rs 5,80,000; with all 5,000 toys on the app he would earn 5,000 x 110 = Rs 5,50,000, which is Rs 30,000 less, and he would also lose the shops that reach buyers who shop in person. So he should not.
s: (a) 50 toys per shop (3,000 / 60)
(b) Aggregator, which stores, packs and delivers to online buyers
(c) Distributors, because distance and terrain make it hard for wholesalers to reach many retailers
(d) Wholesaler Rs 120 against app Rs 110 a toy; all on the app gives Rs 5,50,000 against Rs 5,80,000 now, so he should not

questions.q: Ima Keithal, the Mother's Market, is a unique market in which city?
questions.a: Imphal, Manipur: Ima Keithal means Mother's Market in the Meitei language.

questions.q: About how many women own and run all the shops in Ima Keithal?
questions.a: About 3,000 women own and run all the shops in the market.

questions.q: Over a year, more and more parents in a city ask shops for school bags made from recycled plastic. Going by the chapter, what is the most likely result?
o: Producers take this as a sign of what buyers want and make more such bags
Producers stop making all school bags, because buyers have become choosy
Shops refuse the request, because only producers decide what is made
The government begins making school bags for all children
questions.a: Producers get an indication of what consumers would buy and produce more recycled bags, just as rising demand for refrigerators that use less electricity led producers to make energy-efficient ones.

questions.q: True or False? 'Like guavas, every product has many local buyers and sellers, so a seller can always find a buyer easily.' Give the verdict and correct the statement using the chapter.
questions.a: False. Some products, such as the oil paintings of the artist Aakriti, have fewer local buyers and sellers, so she finds it difficult to find buyers and to decide a price.
s: States the verdict: False
Corrects it: some products such as artwork have few buyers and sellers, so finding a buyer is hard

questions.q: State two ways in which markets help people in their economic life.
questions.a: (1) Markets facilitate transactions between producers and consumers. (2) They help individuals, households and businesses get goods and services that they need but cannot produce themselves.
s: Markets make transactions between producers and consumers possible
Markets help people get goods and services they cannot produce themselves

questions.q: About Ima Keithal: (a) In which language is it called 'Ima Keithal', and what does the name mean in English? (b) Name any two things sold there. (c) Give one way it helps families earn and one way it brings people together.
questions.a: (a) In the Meitei language of Manipur; it means Mother's Market. (b) Any two of: vegetables, clothes including traditional Manipuri attire, handloom and handicrafts, local produce, daily essentials. (c) It provides employment and is an important source of income for thousands of families; it is a melting pot of cultures where people from different communities exchange ideas and enjoy shared traditions.
s: (a) Meitei language; Mother's Market
(b) Names two goods, such as vegetables and handloom
(c) Gives one earning role (employment, income) and one social role (melting pot of cultures)

questions.q: Dolma's family in Darjeeling grows only tea. Using the chapter, show three different ways in which markets help her family live well.
questions.a: (1) Markets let the family sell its tea, a transaction between producer and consumer that brings income. (2) With that money the family buys rice, dal, clothes and other goods it cannot produce itself. (3) Markets also build relationships: the family may keep a monthly account with a trusted local grocer, settled at the end of the month, which carries on over the years.
s: Selling tea through the market, a transaction that earns income
Buying goods and services the family cannot produce itself
A relationship or non-economic role, such as a monthly account with a trusted grocer

questions.q: The chapter opens with Adam Smith's words: 'Prosperity emanates from the market that develops when people need goods and services that they can't create themselves.' (a) Explain the statement in your own words. (b) Support it with two examples from the chapter. (c) Give one case from the chapter where a ready market does not develop easily. (d) Judge whether the statement is true for every product, giving a reason.
questions.a: (a) Wealth grows when markets form because people need things they cannot make themselves, and the market brings buyers and sellers together. (b) Any two: families buy rice, wheat, dal and vegetables that farmers bring to the market; the cloth makers of Surat buy cotton they do not grow through cotton mandis; the Hampi Bazaar prospered through a wide variety of goods traded there. (c) Artwork, such as Aakriti's oil paintings, has fewer local buyers and sellers, so she struggles to find buyers. (d) It is true in general, because markets let producers sell and buyers get what they cannot make; but not equally for every product, because where buyers are few, as with paintings, a market does not develop easily and prosperity is harder to reach.
s: (a) Explains that markets, and wealth, grow from people needing things they cannot make
(b) First supporting example, such as farmers' produce bought by families
(b) Second supporting example, such as Surat's cloth makers buying cotton through mandis
(c) A product without a ready market, such as Aakriti's paintings
(d) A reasoned judgment: true in general but weaker where buyers are few

questions.q: Which of these government actions mainly protects BUYERS rather than sellers or workers?
o: An upper limit on the price of a lifesaving drug
A minimum price at which wheat can be sold
A minimum price for paddy and maize
Minimum wages for work done by employees
questions.a: An upper limit on the price of a lifesaving drug protects buyers from being charged too much. Minimum prices for crops protect farmers from losses, and minimum wages protect workers.

questions.q:
Match each government action in Column I with the example in Column II that the chapter gives for it.
Column I: 1. Setting a maximum price  2. Setting a minimum price  3. Approval procedures and sample testing  4. Strict regulations against pollution
Column II: P. Wheat, paddy and maize  Q. Single-use plastics  R. Lifesaving drugs  S. Medicines made by pharmaceutical companies
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: Maximum price: lifesaving drugs; minimum price: wheat, paddy and maize; approval and sample testing: medicines; strict regulations: single-use plastics that pollute.

questions.q: An asthma inhaler costs its makers about Rs 150 each to produce. A group asks the government to set its maximum price at Rs 20. One member says, 'True or False? The lower the maximum price on a medicine, the better it is for everyone.' Give the verdict and a reason from the chapter.
questions.a: False. A maximum price protects buyers of lifesaving drugs, but the chapter says price limits must be set carefully: if the price is too low, producers would not have any motivation to produce. At Rs 20, below the Rs 150 cost, makers may stop making the inhaler, and patients would not get it at all.
s: States the verdict: False
Reason: too low a price leaves producers no motivation to produce, so the medicine may not be supplied

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The government sets a minimum price at which wheat, paddy and maize can be sold.
Reason (R): This ensures that farmers do not incur losses.
Choose the correct option.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both are true and R explains A: the minimum price for these crops is set so that farmers do not incur losses.

questions.q:
A state government puts up a notice with four orders. Order 1: A heart medicine, a lifesaving drug, cannot be sold above Rs 120 a strip. Order 2: Paddy will be bought from farmers at a fixed minimum price. Order 3: Workers in shops must be paid at least Rs 500 a day. Order 4: Officers will check that each sealed packet of flour holds the net quantity printed on it.
(a) Which order sets a maximum price?
(b) Whom does Order 2 protect, and from what?
(c) What is the purpose of Order 3?
(d) Which government task from the chapter does Order 4 carry out?
questions.a: (a) Order 1, the upper limit on the price of a lifesaving drug. (b) It protects farmers, so that they do not incur losses. (c) It sets a minimum wage so that employers make fair payments to workers. (d) Monitoring the weights and measures of packaged products to check the net quantity in the package.
s: (a) Order 1, the maximum price on a lifesaving drug
(b) Order 2 protects farmers from losses
(c) Order 3 is a minimum wage so employers pay workers fairly
(d) Order 4 monitors weights and measures, the net quantity in packets

questions.q:
Consider these statements about the government's role in markets.
I. If the government sets a price that is too low, producers may have no motivation to produce.
II. The government provides public goods such as parks and roads because producers expect large profits from them.
III. The government puts in place systems to monitor the weights and measures of packaged products.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. II is wrong: the government provides public goods such as parks, roads and policing because producers do NOT expect to make a profit on them.

questions.q: Name the role of the government, as described in the chapter, in each case and give a one-line reason. (a) A new cough syrup is tested in samples before it can be sold. (b) A town builds a free public library open to everyone. (c) A dye factory is ordered to clean its waste water before letting it into the river.
questions.a: (a) Ensuring quality and safety standards: the government sets approval procedures and conducts sample testing of medicines so there is no risk to consumers' health. (b) Providing public goods: a library open to all is a service producers would not expect to profit from, so the government provides it. (c) Mitigating the external effects of markets: the factory's production pollutes the environment, so the government brings in strict regulations to reduce the harm.
s: (a) Quality and safety standards, through approval and sample testing of medicines
(b) Providing public goods that producers would not supply for profit
(c) Mitigating external effects of markets, through strict regulation of pollution

questions.q:
A town council proposes to close its 40 private vegetable shops and sell all vegetables itself through 4 council shops. A nearby town did exactly this last year. Its data: before, 40 shops were open from 7 am to 10 pm and buyers waited about 5 minutes; after, 4 council shops were open from 9 am to 5 pm and buyers waited about 45 minutes. Tomatoes cost Rs 30 per kg both before and after. Running the shops cost that council Rs 12 lakh a year, money it had earlier spent on repairing its roads and park.
(a) From the data, what got worse for buyers, and what stayed the same?
(b) According to the chapter, how do markets usually function, and when does the government step in?
(c) Which warning in the chapter does the nearby town's experience illustrate?
(d) Roads and parks are public goods. Why does the chapter say the government should provide them, and what did that town lose?
(e) Should the council go ahead? Decide, weighing the data, and say what it should do instead.
questions.a: (a) Worse: shop hours fell from 15 to 8 a day and the wait rose from about 5 to 45 minutes, 9 times as long. Same: the tomato price stayed at Rs 30 per kg. (b) Markets function through demand from buyers and supply by sellers; the government steps in where this may not work well, for example to control some prices, ensure quality and safety, or check weights and measures. (c) Too many rules, or too much government control, can make it difficult for markets to function properly. (d) Producers do not expect to make a profit on public goods like roads and parks, so the government provides them; that town took Rs 12 lakh a year away from its roads and park. (e) No. Buyers gained nothing on price, lost hours and waiting time, and the town lost money for public goods. The council should let the private shops sell, and use its role to regulate them (check weights, quality and fair prices) and to provide public goods.
s: (a) Hours down from 15 to 8, waiting up from 5 to 45 minutes; tomato price unchanged at Rs 30
(b) Markets work through demand and supply; the government steps in only where this does not work well
(c) Too many rules make it difficult for markets to function properly
(d) Government provides public goods producers will not profit on; the town lost Rs 12 lakh a year for roads and park
(e) Decides against the plan using the data, and proposes regulating shops and funding public goods instead

questions.q: A brick kiln near a town makes 2,00,000 bricks a month and sells them to builders, who are happy with the bricks and their price. Its profit is Rs 1 a brick. Smoke from its chimney causes breathing illness, and the town clinic treats about 200 such patients a month. The government is weighing two plans. The closure plan: close the kiln, so its 80 workers lose their jobs. The chimney plan: make the kiln fit a cleaner chimney costing Rs 50,000 a month, which is expected to cut these patients by 70%. (a) Who are the seller and the buyers in the brick market, and who is affected without being part of it? (b) Under the chimney plan, what would the kiln's monthly profit be? (c) Under the chimney plan, about how many such patients a month would the clinic expect? (d) Which plan should the government make? Justify, using your answers and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) The kiln is the seller and the builders are the buyers; the townspeople who fall ill are affected though they take no part in the brick market, an effect beyond buying and selling. (b) 2,00,000 x Rs 1 - Rs 50,000 = Rs 1,50,000 a month, so the kiln is still profitable. (c) 70% fewer: 200 x 0.3 = about 60 patients (140 fewer). (d) The chimney plan. The chapter says the government intervenes with strict regulations to mitigate the negative effects of markets; The chimney plan cuts the harm sharply while the kiln stays profitable, the 80 jobs are kept and builders still get bricks. Closing the kiln would remove the harm but also the jobs and the bricks.
s: (a) Kiln sells, builders buy; the townspeople fall ill outside the transaction
(c) About 60 patients a month (200 x 30%)
(d) Chooses the chimney plan, justified by regulation to mitigate harm while profit and jobs remain

questions.q: What does FSSAI, the mark seen on food packets, stand for?
o: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India
Food Supply and Storage Agency of India
Fair Sales and Standards Association of India
Farm Seeds and Spices Authority of India
questions.a: Food Safety and Standards Authority of India; its mark shows the food has been tested by the government and is safe to consume.

questions.q: Which of these products is most likely to carry the AGMARK certification?
questions.a: A packet of pulses: AGMARK (Ag for agriculture) certifies agricultural products such as vegetables, fruits, cereals, pulses, spices and honey.

questions.q:
Match each mark in Column I with what it tells a buyer in Column II.
Column I: 1. FSSAI  2. ISI  3. AGMARK  4. BEE Star rating
Column II: P. The certification mark for agricultural products such as cereals and spices  Q. How energy efficient an appliance is; more stars mean less electricity  R. The food has been tested by the government and is safe to consume  S. Issued by the Bureau of Indian Standards for products like electrical appliances, construction materials and tyres
Choose the correct matching.
questions.a: FSSAI = food tested and safe; ISI = Bureau of Indian Standards mark for appliances, construction materials and tyres; AGMARK = agricultural products; BEE Star = energy efficiency.

questions.q: True or False? 'Besides certification marks, online reviews and feedback from other consumers can help a buyer decide whether to buy a product online.' Give the verdict and one more way, from the chapter, in which a product's reputation is built.
questions.a: True. The chapter says online reviews and feedback from other consumers help us decide whether to buy while shopping online. A product's reputation is also built through word of mouth, when friends or relatives suggest it.
s: States the verdict: True
Names word of mouth, such as friends or relatives suggesting a product

questions.q: Name any four details printed on the label of a packet of gram flour, as shown in the chapter.
questions.a: Any four of: net quantity, date of manufacture, best before date, MRP, name and address of the manufacturer, nutrition facts panel, batch number, allergen declaration, FSSAI mark and licence number, ingredients list.
s: Names two correct label details, such as net quantity and MRP
Names two more correct label details, such as best before date and batch number

questions.q: About the BEE Star rating: (a) What does BEE stand for? (b) On which kinds of products is it found? Name two. (c) What does a higher number of stars tell the buyer, and why is that good?
questions.a: (a) Bureau of Energy Efficiency. (b) Electronic items such as TVs, laptops and air conditioners (any two). (c) More stars mean the appliance uses less energy and electricity, so the electricity bill is lower and it is better for the environment.
s: (a) Bureau of Energy Efficiency
(b) Two products such as TVs, laptops or air conditioners
(c) More stars mean less electricity used: a lower bill and good for the environment

questions.q: Aarav is allergic to peanuts. At a shop he picks up a packet of chocolate cookies that carries the FSSAI logo and licence number. Which detail on the label should he read before buying, going by the chapter's packet label?
o: The allergen declaration, which names substances in the food that can cause an allergy
The FSSAI mark, because a food tested by the government is safe for every buyer
The nutrition facts panel, because it lists the fat, sugar and protein in the cookies
The batch number, because it shows which factory lot the packet came from
questions.a: The allergen declaration. The FSSAI mark shows that the food has been tested and is safe to consume in general; it does not tell a buyer with a peanut allergy whether the cookies contain peanuts. The allergen declaration on the label does.

questions.q:
The Sharma family buys red chilli powder online in 500 g packets and uses about 6 kg a year. Packet P costs Rs 90 and carries both the AGMARK and the FSSAI marks; it has 4.2 stars from 2,000 reviews. Packet Q costs Rs 60 and carries no certification mark; it has 5.0 stars from only 3 reviews. The elder son says, 'Q has a perfect score and is cheaper, so it must be the better powder.'
(a) What does each mark on Packet P tell the family?
(b) How much more would the family spend in a year by buying P?
(c) Why is Q's 5.0-star score weak evidence of quality?
(d) Which packet should the family buy? Justify, using the data and the chapter.
questions.a: (a) AGMARK is the certification mark for agricultural products such as spices; FSSAI shows the food has been tested by the government and is safe to consume. (b) 6 kg = 12 packets of 500 g; 12 x (90 - 60) = Rs 360 a year more. (c) Online reviews are the feedback of other consumers, not a government test, and only 3 people have reviewed Q, too few to show what most buyers find; P's score comes from 2,000 buyers. (d) Packet P: its marks confirm that it meets minimum quality standards and is safe to eat, and many buyers rate it well. The extra Rs 360 a year (Rs 30 a month) is small for food the family eats every day.
s: (a) AGMARK: certified agricultural product such as a spice; FSSAI: tested and safe to consume
(b) Rs 360 a year (12 packets x Rs 30)
(c) Reviews are consumer opinions, not a government test, and 3 reviews are too few
(d) Chooses P, justified by the certification marks, the larger review base and the small extra cost

questions.q:
A school is building a new classroom block on a budget of Rs 20 lakh and needs 250 bags of cement. Brand A carries the ISI mark and costs Rs 400 a bag. Brand B carries no mark and costs Rs 340 a bag. The contractor says, 'I have used Brand B on many houses; people in my area speak well of it.'
(a) Which mark should the school look for on cement, and what does it ensure?
(b) Which body issues this mark?
(c) How much more will Brand A cost for 250 bags, and what percentage of the budget is this?
(d) The contractor's advice is which way of judging quality, according to the chapter? What is its limit here?
(e) Which brand should the school buy? Decide, weighing the data and who will use the building.
questions.a: (a) The ISI mark, which the chapter says is found on construction materials; it ensures quality and that the product is safe to use. (b) The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS). (c) 250 x (400 - 340) = Rs 15,000, which is 15,000 / 20,00,000 x 100 = 0.75% of the budget. (d) Reputation built through word of mouth; it is the opinion of people who used the cement, not a government check that it meets minimum quality standards. (e) Brand A: hundreds of children will use the building for years, so a cement certified for quality and safety matters more than a saving of Rs 15,000, which is less than 1% of the budget.
s: (a) ISI mark: ensures quality and that the product is safe to use
(b) Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS)
(c) Rs 15,000 extra, 0.75% of Rs 20 lakh
(d) Word of mouth or reputation; an opinion, not a certification of minimum quality
(e) Chooses Brand A, weighing children's safety against a cost under 1% of the budget
